sections.title: Feeling as a function
sections.line: Jung's definition of feeling: CW6 ¶723 and ¶724.

quotes.text: I count feeling among the four basic psychological functions (q.v.).

I am unable to support the psychological school that considers feeling a secondary phenomenon dependent on “representations” or sensations, but in company with Höffding, Wundt, Lehmann, Külpe, Baldwin, and others, I regard it as an independent function sui generis.”

Feeling is primarily a process that takes place between the ego (q.v.) and a given content, a process, moreover, that imparts to the content a definite value in the sense of acceptance or rejection (“like” or “dislike”).

sections.title: Judgment; rational and irrational feeling
sections.line: Feeling as judgment, directed and undirected feeling, and the thinking type: CW6 ¶725, ¶729 and ¶905.

quotes.text: Hence feeling is a kind of judgment, differing from intellectual judgment in that its aim is not to establish conceptual relations but to set up a subjective criterion of acceptance or rejection.

Strictly speaking, therefore, only active, directed feeling should be termed rational, whereas passive feeling is irrational (q.v.) in so far as it confers values without the participation or even against the intentions of the subject.
The latter would be undirected, passive feeling, as these expressions themselves show: the one is an activity, the other a passive state. Undirected feeling is feeling-intuition.

The thinking type, for instance, must necessarily repress and exclude feeling as far as possible, since nothing disturbs thinking so much as feeling, and the feeling type represses thinking, since nothing is more injurious to feeling than thinking.

quotes.text: This I regard as one of the four basic psychological functions (q.v.). Thinking is the psychological function which, following its own laws, brings the contents of ideation into conceptual connection with one another.

Under sensation I include all perceptions by means of the sense organs; by thinking I mean the function of intellectual cognition and the forming of logical conclusions; feeling is a function of subjective valuation; intuition I take as perception by way of the unconscious, or perception of unconscious contents.

quotes.text: Further, I call directed thinking a rational (q.v.) function, because it arranges the contents of ideation under concepts in accordance with a rational norm of which I am conscious.

Sensation and intuition I call irrational functions, because they are both concerned simply with what happens and with actual or potential realities. Thinking and feeling, being discriminative functions, are rational.

The thinking type, for instance, must necessarily repress and exclude feeling as far as possible, since nothing disturbs thinking so much as feeling, and the feeling type represses thinking, since nothing is more injurious to feeling than thinking.

as Venus here rules Aquarius, weakness

sections.line: Crowley on the title and the sign Scorpio (pdf p178); on the Sun (pdf p203).

quotes.text: The Six of Cups is called Pleasure.
The zodiacal sign governing the card being Scorpio, pleasure is here rooted in its most convenient soil.
This influence is fortified by that of the Sun, who also represents the Six.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree
sections.line: Crowley on the Sixes and Tiphareth, and on Tiphareth and the Sun (pdf p177).

quotes.text: These cards are attributed to Tiphareth.
In the planetary system it represents the Sun; in the system of Tetragrammaton it represents the Son.

sections.title: What the card figures
sections.line: Crowley on Pleasure in its highest sense (pdf p203).

quotes.text: Pleasure, in the title of this card, must be understood in its highest sense: it implies well‐being, harmony of natural forces without effort or strain, ease, satisfaction.

family:thoth-six-of-disks.line: Crowley’s Six of Disks: Success (pdf p178); the Moon in Taurus (pdf p232); Tiphareth (pdf p177, p232).

sections.title: Title and attribution
sections.line: Crowley on the title (pdf p178); on the Moon in Taurus (pdf p232).

quotes.text: The Six of Disks is called Success; the ruler is the Moon.
The Moon in Taurus rules the card; and this, while increasing the approach to perfection (for the Moon is exalted in Taurus and therefore in her highest form) marks that the condition is transient.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree
sections.line: Crowley on the Sixes and Tiphareth (pdf p177); on the Number Six, Tiphareth (pdf p232).

quotes.text: These cards are attributed to Tiphareth.
The Number Six, Tiphareth, as before, represents the full harmonious establishment of the Energy of the Element.

family:thoth-six-of-swords.line: Crowley’s Six of Swords: Science (pdf p178); Mercury in Aquarius (pdf p218); Tiphareth (pdf p177, p211).

sections.title: Title and attribution
sections.line: Crowley on the title (pdf p178); on Mercury in Aquarius (pdf p218).

quotes.text: The Six of Swords is called Science.
Mercury, in Aquarius, represents the celestial Energy influencing the Kerub of the Man, thus showing intelligence and humanity.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree
sections.line: Crowley on Tiphareth as the airy Sephira (pdf p211); on the Sixes and Tiphareth (pdf p177).

quotes.text: The Ruach is centred in the airy Sephira, Tiphareth, who is the Son, the first‐born of the Father, and the Sun, the first emanation of the creative Phallus.
These cards are attributed to Tiphareth.

sections.title: What the card figures
sections.line: Crowley on the balance of the mental and moral faculties (pdf p218).

quotes.text: The perfect balance of all mental and moral faculties, hardly won, and almost impossible to hold in an ever‐changing world, declares the idea of Science in its fullest interpretation.

family:thoth-six-of-wands.line: Crowley’s Six of Wands: Victory (pdf p178); Jupiter and Leo (pdf p191); Tiphareth (pdf p177, p191).

sections.title: Title and attribution
sections.line: Crowley on the title (pdf p178); on Jupiter and Leo (pdf p191).

quotes.text: The four Sixes are thus representative of their respective elements at their practical The Six of Wands is called Victory.
The reference is also to Jupiter and Leo, which seems to imply a benediction on the harmony and beauty of this arrangement.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree
sections.line: Crowley on the Sixes and Tiphareth (pdf p177); on Tiphareth of the suit of Fire (pdf p191).

quotes.text: These cards are attributed to Tiphareth.
This card represents Tiphareth of the suit of Fire.

family:thoth-star.line: Crowley on Atu XVII: the letter Hé, Aquarius, Nuith our Lady of the Stars, and the Path of Hé (pdf p100, p101, p211).

sections.title: Letter, sign and picture
sections.line: Crowley on the letter Hé, Aquarius, and Nuith, our Lady of the Stars (pdf p100).

quotes.text: This card is attributed to the letter Hé, as has been explained elsewhere. It refers to the Zodiacal sign of Aquarius, the water‐ bearer.
The picture represents Nuith, our Lady of the Stars.

sections.title: The figure of Nuith
sections.line: Crowley on the figure personified as human-seeming (pdf p100) and on heaven as a veil before the face of the goddess (pdf p101).

quotes.text: In this card she is definitely personified as a human‐seeming figure; she is represented as bearing two cups, one golden, held high above her head, from which she pours water upon it.
Heaven itself is no more than a veil before the face of the immortal goddess.

sections.title: The Path of Hé
sections.line: Crowley on the Path of Hé, the Great Mother, the Star, our Lady Nuit (pdf p211), and on Chokmah and Tiphareth (pdf p67).

quotes.text: From his father, Chokmah, he is informed though the Path of Hé, the Great Mother, the Star, our Lady Nuit, so that the creative impulse is communicated to him by all possibilities soever.
His authority is derived from Chokmah, the creative Wisdom, the Word, and is exerted upon Tiphareth, the organized man.

quotes.text: THE SUN This card represents, in heraldic language, “the Sun, charged with a rose, on a mount vert”.1
This is one of the simplest of the cards; it represents Heru‐ra‐ha, the Lord of the New Aeon, in his manifestation to the race of men as the Sun spiritual, moral, and physical.

sections.title: The rose and the Rose and Cross
sections.line: Crowley on the rose as the flowering of the solar influence (pdf p105) and on the broadening of the idea of the Rose and Cross (pdf p106).

The card itself symbolizes this broadening of the idea of the Rose and Cross.

quotes.text: These paths are the paths which join the ten numbers on the figure called the Tree of Life.
Because that is the number of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and one letter goes to each path.

In nature, the obvious symbol of Air is the Wind “which bloweth whithersoever it listeth”.

sections.title: The Vau of the Ace
sections.line: Crowley on the Ace of Swords as the Essence of the Vau of Tetragrammaton (pdf p210) and on the Princes as the Forces of the letter Vau (pdf p139).

The Princes represent the Forces of the letter Vau in the Name.

It is necessitated, as will appear later, by the structure of the universe, and in particular of the Solar System, as symbolized by the Holy Qabalah.

sections.line: Crowley on the title (pdf p181); on Mercury in Virgo (pdf p237).

quotes.text: The Ten of Disks is called Wealth.
Mercury rules this card in Virgo; and this may imply that the acquired wealth, being inert, will be dissipated unless put to further use by devoting its power to objects other than mere accumulation.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree
sections.line: Crowley on the Tens and Malkuth, and on Malkuth in the world of Assiah (pdf p181).

quotes.text: These cards are attributed to Malkuth.
So far as the Sephira is concerned, it is right down in the world of Assiah.

sections.title: What the card figures
sections.line: Crowley on the card as a hieroglyph of the cycle of regeneration (pdf p237).

quotes.text: This card is in fact a hieroglyph of the cycle of regeneration.

sections.line: Crowley on the planetary attribution of the Tens (pdf p181); on the coin in the place of Hod (pdf p237).

quotes.text: There is now no planetary attribution to consider.
These disks are inscribed with various symbols of mercurial character, except that the coin in the place of Hod (Mercury) on the Tree is marked with the cipher of the Sun.

family:thoth-ten-of-swords.line: Crowley’s Ten of Swords: Ruin (pdf p181); the Sun in Gemini (pdf p222); Malkuth (pdf p181).

sections.line: Crowley on the title (pdf p181); on the Sun in Gemini (pdf p222).

quotes.text: The Ten of Swords is called Ruin.
The card is also ruled by the Sun in Gemini, but the mercurial airy quality of the Sign serves to disperse his rays; this card shows the disruption and disorder of harmonious and stable energy.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree
sections.line: Crowley on the Tens and Malkuth, and on Malkuth in the world of Assiah (pdf p181).

quotes.text: These cards are attributed to Malkuth.
So far as the Sephira is concerned, it is right down in the world of Assiah.

quotes.text: There is now no planetary attribution to consider.

family:thoth-three-of-cups.line: Crowley’s Three of Cups: Lord of Abundance (pdf p176); Binah and Mercury in Cancer (pdf p199).

sections.title: Title and suit
sections.line: Crowley on the card’s title (pdf p176); on the suit and its element (pdf p24).

quotes.text: The Three of Cups is called the Lord of Abundance.
The four suits are named as follows: “Wands”, attributed to Fire; “Cups”, to Water; “Swords”, to Air; and “Disks” (“Coins”, or “Pantacles”), to Earth.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree and in the zodiac
sections.line: Crowley on Binah in the suit of Water and on Mercury in Cancer (pdf p199).

quotes.text: This card refers to Binah in the suit of Water.
The card is referred to the influence of Mercury in Cancer; this carries further the above thesis.

sections.title: What it figures
sections.line: Crowley on the card as the spiritual basis of fertility, and on Binah, the Great Sea (pdf p199).

quotes.text: It is the spiritual basis of fertility.
Binah, the Great Sea, is the Moon in one aspect, but Saturn in another; and Mercury, besides being the Word or Will of the All‐One, is the guide of the souls of the Dead.

family:thoth-three-of-disks.line: Crowley’s Three of Disks: Lord of Work (pdf p176); Binah and Mars in Capricornus (pdf p228).

sections.title: Title and suit
sections.line: Crowley on the card’s title (pdf p176); on the suit and its element (pdf p24).

quotes.text: The Three of Pentacles, in a similar manner, exhibits the result of the idea of Earth, of the crystallization of forces; and so the Three of Pentacles is called the Lord of Work.
The four suits are named as follows: “Wands”, attributed to Fire; “Cups”, to Water; “Swords”, to Air; and “Disks” (“Coins”, or “Pantacles”), to Earth.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree and in the zodiac
sections.line: Crowley on Binah in the sphere of Earth (pdf p228); on the Threes and Binah (pdf p176); on Mars in Capricornus (pdf p228).

quotes.text: The influence of Binah in the sphere of Earth shows the material establishment of the idea of the Universe, the determination of its basic form.
These cards are referred to Binah; in each of them is expressed the symbolism of Understanding.
It is ruled by Mars in Capricornus; he is exalted in that Sign, and therefore at his best.

sections.title: What it figures
sections.line: Crowley on the energy of Mars as constructive and on the pyramid viewed from above the apex (pdf p228).

quotes.text: His energy is constructive, like that of the builder or engineer.
The card represents a pyramid viewed from above the apex.

family:thoth-three-of-swords.line: Crowley’s Three of Swords: Lord of Sorrow (pdf p176); Binah and Saturn in Libra (pdf p214).

sections.title: Title and suit
sections.line: Crowley on the card’s title (pdf p176); on the suit and its element (pdf p24).

quotes.text: The idea of division, of mutability, the idea of the airy quality of things, manifests itself in the Three of Swords, the Lord of Sorrow.
The four suits are named as follows: “Wands”, attributed to Fire; “Cups”, to Water; “Swords”, to Air; and “Disks” (“Coins”, or “Pantacles”), to Earth.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree and in the zodiac
sections.line: Crowley on Binah in the realm of Air and on Saturn in Libra (pdf p214).

quotes.text: Binah, the Great Mother, here rules the realm of Air.
This is accentuated by the Celestial Lordship of Saturn in Libra.

sections.title: What it figures
sections.line: Crowley on the card as the womb of Chaos (pdf p214); on Weltschmerz (pdf p176).

quotes.text: This card is dark and heavy; it is, so to speak, the womb of Chaos.
It is Weltschmerz, the universal sorrow; it is the quality of melancholy.

family:thoth-three-of-wands.line: Crowley’s Three of Wands: Lord of Virtue (pdf p176); Binah and the Sun in Aries (pdf p187).

sections.title: Title and suit
sections.line: Crowley on the card’s title (pdf p176); on the suit and its element (pdf p24).

quotes.text: The Three of Wands is accordingly the Lord of Virtue.
The four suits are named as follows: “Wands”, attributed to Fire; “Cups”, to Water; “Swords”, to Air; and “Disks” (“Coins”, or “Pantacles”), to Earth.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree and in the zodiac
sections.line: Crowley on Binah in the suit of Fire and on the Sun in Aries (pdf p187).

quotes.text: This card refers to Binah in the suit of Fire, and so represents the establishment of primeval Energy.
It refers to the Sun in Aries, the Sign in which he is exalted.

sections.title: What it figures
sections.line: Crowley on the Threes and Understanding (pdf p176); on the wand as a Lotus in blossom (pdf p187).

quotes.text: These cards are referred to Binah; in each of them is expressed the symbolism of Understanding.
For this reason one sees the wand taking the form of the Lotus in blossom.

quotes.text: This card is attributed to the letter Pé, which means a mouth; it refers to the planet Mars.
The picture shows the destruction of existing material by fire.

sections.title: The Paths and the letters
sections.line: Crowley on the Paths that join the ten numbers on the Tree of Life and on one letter to each path (pdf p36).

Because that is the number of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and one letter goes to each path.

The dominating feature of this card is the Eye of Horus.

sections.title: What it figures
sections.line: Crowley on the Two as the Word and the Will, and on the harmony of the male and the female (pdf p197).

quotes.text: The Two always represents the Word and the Will. It is the first manifestation.
It shows the harmony of the male and the female: interpreted in the largest sense.

sections.title: Its place on the Tree
sections.line: Crowley on the Two and Chokmah in the suit of Earth (pdf p227); on the Twos and Chokmah (pdf p35).

quotes.text: The number Two, Chokmah, here rules in the suit pertaining to Earth.
The 2 pertains to Chokmah.

sections.title: What it figures
sections.line: Crowley on the card as the picture of the manifested Universe and on the interplay of the Four Elements (pdf p227).

quotes.text: One may in fact consider the card as the picture of the complete manifested Universe, in respect of its dynamics.
They thus represent the harmonious interplay of the Four Elements in constant movement.

Its celestial rulers are Jupiter and Capricornus; and these symbols are most inharmonious, so that in practical matters the good fortune of Jupiter is very limited.

sections.title: Letter, planet and element

quotes.text: The letter Tau is attributed to Saturn, the outermost and slowest of the seven sacred planets; because of these dull, heavy qualities, the element of earth was thrust upon the symbol.
The letter Tau is attributed to Saturn, the outermost and slowest of the seven sacred planets; because of these dull, heavy qualities, the element of earth was thrust upon the symbol.

sections.title: The path of Tau and the Great Work
sections.line: Crowley on the path of Tau as an emanation from the Moon of Yesod descending upon Malkuth, on the Great Work accomplished, and on the Fool and the Universe (pdf p110).

quotes.text: Saturn, therefore, is masculine; he is the old god, the god of fertility) the sun in the south; but equally the Great Sea, the great Mother; and the letter Tau upon the Tree of Life appears as an emanation from the moon of Yesod, the foundation of the Tree and representative of the reproductive process and of the equilibrium between change and stability, or rather their identification. The influence of the path descends upon the earth, Malkuth, the daughter.
